question_text: What are disproportionation reactions? Give an example.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: A disproportionation reaction is a redox
reaction in which the same element, in one
steps.why: The defining point is one element starting in one oxidation state and ending in two — one higher (oxidation) and one lower (reduction) — in the same reaction.
common_mistakes: Writing only that oxidation and reduction happen together. That is every redox reaction. Here the SAME element does both.
Leaving out that the element starts in a single oxidation state.
steps.memory_tip: Dis- means splitting apart: one oxidation state splits into a higher one and a lower one.
steps.margin_note: The words same element, oxidised and reduced must all appear.

steps.label: The example
lines: Chlorine in Cl₂ has oxidation number 0.
It decreases to −1 in Cl⁻ (reduction) and
steps.why: The example must show the one starting oxidation number (0 in Cl₂) and the two products with a lower number (−1) and a higher number (+5). Writing the three numbers is what proves disproportionation.
common_mistakes: Writing the equation without the oxidation numbers 0, −1 and +5.
Copying the equation unbalanced. Check: 6 Cl, 6 O and 6 H on each side, charge −6 on each side.
steps.memory_tip: Chlorine in alkali: 0 splits into −1 and +5.
steps.margin_note: Mark the oxidation numbers above Cl₂, Cl⁻ and ClO₃⁻ — that display earns the mark.

insider_note: The definition alone earns only one mark. The examiner looks for the three oxidation numbers 0, −1 and +5 written over the example equation.
